title: Quality control
blurb: Define quality control: inspecting, measuring and testing outputs to verify they meet the acceptance criteria.
question: Before a new housing estate is handed over, inspectors check every home against the agreed acceptance criteria and find three with missing loft insulation, which are sent back for rework and re-inspected. Which quality activity is this, and what makes it different from quality assurance?

teach.body: Quality control is the inspection, measurement and testing that verifies the project's outputs meet the acceptance criteria defined in quality planning. In plain English: you take the actual deliverable, check it against the agreed criteria, and find anything that does not conform. Quality control is product-focused, it detects defects, and it is usually carried out by the project team or by inspectors.

Inspect: look at the output (a surveyor walks through a finished home). Measure: compare dimensions or values with the specification (a gauge checks the width of new rail track). Test: make the output perform and see whether it works (testers run a new app's checkout). Each one checks the PRODUCT against the acceptance criteria. None of them looks at whether the team followed its procedures: that is assurance.

Greenfield Homes is handing over 40 houses. The acceptance criteria (set in quality planning) include insulation depth, window seals and electrical safety certificates. Before handover an inspector checks every house, measures loft insulation and tests the windows. Three homes fail on insulation. They are rejected, reworked and re-inspected until they pass, and every result is recorded. Meanwhile, separately, the PMO checks that the builder's installation procedure is followed: that is assurance, not control.

root.label: Meets acceptance criteria?
root.sub: Compare the output with what was agreed

children.label: Reject or rework
children.sub: Record the defect, fix it, then retest

teach.caption: A failed check is reported and corrected, never ignored and never solved by lowering the criteria.

teach.text: Quality control DETECTS defects in outputs; it does not prevent them by checking processes (that is assurance) and it does not set the criteria (that is planning). And 'independent' does not turn it into assurance: an external inspector testing a product is still doing quality control.

teach.h: Control vs assurance on the housing estate

teach.caption: Defects found late cost more to fix, which is why quality management also plans and assures quality rather than relying on control alone.

items: Quality control: inspection, measurement and testing to verify that outputs meet the acceptance criteria defined in quality planning.
Product-focused and detective: it finds defects in outputs that already exist.
Usually done by the project team or inspectors; results are recorded.
Failed outputs are rejected or reworked and retested, not accepted or excused.
Assurance checks the process; control checks the product.

summary: You can now define quality control as the inspection, measurement and testing of outputs against the acceptance criteria set in quality planning. You can also explain why it is product-focused and detective, and tell it apart from quality assurance.

A.q: Which of the following best defines quality control?
options: Setting the quality standards that outputs must meet
Inspecting and testing outputs against criteria
Checking the team follows agreed procedures
Capturing lessons learned at project closure
A.why: Quality control is the inspection, measurement and testing that verifies outputs meet the acceptance criteria.

whyNot.0: Setting standards and criteria is quality planning.
whyNot.2: Checking that agreed procedures are followed is quality assurance.
whyNot.3: Capturing lessons at closure is the job of a post-project review.

A.q: Against what does quality control verify the project's outputs?
A.why: Quality control verifies that outputs meet the acceptance criteria defined in quality planning.

whyNot.1: The communication plan sets out who gets what information; it holds no output criteria.
whyNot.2: The stakeholder register lists stakeholders, not the conditions outputs must meet.
whyNot.3: A benefits profile describes expected benefits, which are reviewed separately.

A.q: Which pair of words best describes quality control?
A.why: Quality control examines the product and detects defects in outputs that already exist.

whyNot.0: Process and prevention describe quality assurance.
whyNot.1: Benefits and realisation belong to benefits management and benefits reviews.
whyNot.3: Governance and approval describe decision gates and the governance board.

B.q: Testers run 200 test cases on a new payroll system and log 12 failures for the developers to fix. Which quality activity is this?
B.why: Testing the actual output and logging failures against expected results is quality control.

whyNot.0: Quality planning would have defined the tests and criteria, not run them.
whyNot.1: Quality assurance checks the process being followed, not the system itself.
whyNot.3: Change control manages requests to change the baseline, not defects found in testing.

B.q: Who typically carries out quality control on a project?
options: The sponsor at each decision gate
The end users after benefits review
B.why: Quality control is usually carried out by the project team or by inspectors who check the outputs.

whyNot.0: The sponsor makes decisions at gates; they do not inspect and test outputs.
whyNot.2: Auditors of process provide assurance, not control.
whyNot.3: A benefits review comes after closure; quality control happens as outputs are produced.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are quality control activities?
1. Measuring a finished part against its tolerances
2. Auditing whether the agreed method was used
3. Testing a new app's checkout before release
4. Agreeing the acceptance criteria with users
B.why: Measuring a part and testing an app both check the actual outputs, so both are quality control.

whyNot.1: Statement 4 is quality planning: it sets the criteria rather than checking against them.
whyNot.2: Statement 2 is quality assurance: it audits the method, not the output.
whyNot.3: Neither statement is control: 2 is assurance and 4 is planning.

C.q: Quality control finds that 5 of 40 new windows fail a leak test. Which response best fits the purpose of quality control?
options: Accept all 40, as most windows passed
Lower the acceptance criteria to fit
Pass the windows to assurance to test
Rework or reject the 5 and retest
C.why: Outputs that fail their acceptance criteria are rejected or reworked and then retested until they conform.

whyNot.0: Accepting failed outputs defeats the purpose of checking them.
whyNot.1: Changing criteria to suit a faulty output undermines quality; criteria change only through change control.
whyNot.2: Assurance checks processes; testing the windows is control's job.

C.q: Why is quality control described as detective rather than preventive?
options: It finds defects in outputs that exist
It audits processes before work starts
It sets criteria before defects occur
It investigates the causes of risks
C.why: Quality control inspects and tests outputs that have already been produced, so it detects defects rather than preventing them.

whyNot.1: Auditing processes is quality assurance, which is preventive.
whyNot.3: Investigating risk causes is part of risk management.

C.q: A project has a detailed quality management plan and an independent PMO review of its processes, but nobody inspects or tests the finished outputs. What is missing?
C.why: Inspecting and testing the outputs themselves is quality control, which is absent here.

whyNot.0: Quality planning is in place: there is a quality management plan.
whyNot.1: Quality assurance is in place: the PMO reviews the processes.
whyNot.2: A benefits review looks at benefits after closure, not at whether outputs meet criteria.

reteach.title: Think of a car's MOT test
reteach.question: Every year your car goes for its MOT. The tester checks the brakes, lights and emissions against set standards. Why is that quality control?

blocks.body: The MOT tester does not ask how your garage services cars. They test THIS car against fixed standards: brake efficiency, working lights, emission levels. If it passes, you get a certificate. If it fails, it is repaired and retested. That is exactly quality control: inspect, measure and test the product against agreed criteria, detect any defects, and fix them before acceptance.

blocks.text: If the DVSA audited how the garage runs its MOT procedure, that would be assurance. Testing the car itself is control.

explain.body: Quality control uses three kinds of check on outputs: inspecting them, measuring them and testing them.

test.q: Complete the statement: quality control is the ______, measurement and testing of outputs to verify they meet the acceptance criteria.
test.why: Quality control is the inspection, measurement and testing of outputs against the acceptance criteria.

whyNot.0: Planning comes before control and sets the criteria.
whyNot.1: Authorising is a decision that may follow control, not part of the definition.
whyNot.3: Auditing usually examines processes, which is assurance.

explain.body: Control needs a yardstick. It checks outputs against the acceptance criteria that quality planning defined before the work started.

test.q: Where do the acceptance criteria used in quality control come from?
test.why: Quality planning defines the acceptance criteria that quality control later checks outputs against.

whyNot.0: A benefits review assesses benefits after closure; it does not set output criteria.
whyNot.1: A project audit checks compliance with processes and governance.
whyNot.2: The issue log records problems that have arisen.

explain.body: Control examines the actual product and finds defects that already exist. It does not examine how the work was done.

test.q: On a rail project, which of the following is a quality control activity?
options: Measuring the gauge of new track
test.why: Measuring the actual track checks the product against its criteria, which is quality control.

whyNot.1: Auditing the procedure examines the process, which is quality assurance.
whyNot.2: Writing acceptance criteria is quality planning.
whyNot.3: Reviewing lessons after opening is a post-project review.

explain.body: Control results are recorded. Outputs that meet their criteria can be accepted and signed off; those that fail are reworked and retested.

test.q: After quality control, what happens to an output that meets all its acceptance criteria?
options: It is sent back for further rework
It can be accepted and signed off
It is sent for a benefits review
It triggers a new change request
test.why: An output that meets its acceptance criteria can be accepted and signed off.

whyNot.0: Rework is for outputs that fail their criteria.
whyNot.2: Benefits reviews assess benefits after closure, not individual outputs.
whyNot.3: A change request is raised to change the baseline, not because an output passed.
